title: The smaller array (Sn 4.12)
hookLine: read it: everyone calls their own truth true
tomorrow: so if everyone's arguing, where does the wise one stand?

lines: SO WHICH OF THEM IS RIGHT?
cards: Two hundred replies deep under a cooking video. One person: real carbonara never has cream. Another: my grandmother used cream her whole life.
A third posts a link. A fourth calls everyone clueless. Nobody is changing anybody's mind, and nobody is leaving.
Now step back a long way, into the Buddha's India, and the same thread is running in the town square. Teachers stand in rows, each one certain, each calling the others fools.
And someone turns to the Buddha and asks: so which of them is right?

teach.b: This is the Smaller Array, the twelfth poem in the chapter of eights in the Sutta Nipata. Array, as in troops lined up for battle. The questioner describes the scene.
Each teacher, settled in his own view, says: whoever knows this knows the truth; whoever rejects it is incomplete. They argue, and each calls the other a fool. All of them call themselves experts.
Which one speaks the truth? The Buddha doesn't pick a winner. He turns the question around.

teach.h: IF HE'S A FOOL, ALL ARE FOOLS.
teach.b: If someone who won't accept another's teaching is a fool, then every one of them is a fool, because every one of them holds his own view.
And if holding your own view makes you wise, then nobody in the square is a fool at all. Either way, the name-calling falls apart. Then the line people remember.
Truth is one, the poem says; there is no second, and someone who understands it has nothing to quarrel about. So why are there so many truths in the square?

teach.h: LED BY LOVE OF THEIR OWN VIEW.
teach.b: Because, the poem says, each one is led by love of his own view.
Each calls it true. That's the answer to the cliffhanger. The poem never says which teacher had it right.
It looks at the arguing itself: a crowd of people each holding a mirror and calling it a window.

how: Readers of the Sutta Nipata's chapter of eights often take it a poem at a day, reading it aloud or slowly, and Theravada teachers use its poems on views to talk about holding opinions loosely.

o: a list of the small rules a new monk must learn first
a poem about rows of teachers, each sure he alone is right
a short sermon on how monks should line up for alms

games.q: the smaller array — tap the pairs.
p: which of them speaks the truth?
then all of them are fools
led by love of their own view

s: the poem ends by naming the teacher who had it right
it never names one. it looks at the arguing itself: each one led by love of his own view.
the Buddha turns the insult around: if one is a fool, all are
each holds his own view, so by their own rule every one of them is a fool.
'truth is one' means the poem tells you to win the argument
the poem says one who understands the truth has nothing to quarrel about.

games.q: two coworkers have argued all week about the right way to run a project, each calling the other's plan amateur. they ask you to settle it. what would the smaller array do first?
o: point out that each is calling their own plan true, and ask what the project needs.
pick the stronger plan; the poem says truth is one, so one of them must be right.
tell them every plan is equally good, so the whole thing is just opinion.
games.why: the Buddha didn't crown a winner or say every view is fine. he showed that each side, by its own rule, was a fool, and that love of one's own view was doing the arguing.

practice: Bring to mind one opinion you hold firmly, something small enough to be safe. Now, quietly, out loud, say the best single sentence the other side would say for theirs, the way they'd say it, so that they would nod.
Then rest with your breath and notice what it's like to have spoken it.

wordCard.voice: The Smaller Array: Sutta Nipata 4.12, a poem about rows of teachers, each sure, each calling the others fools. The Buddha answers by looking at the arguing, not by crowning a winner.

orig.note: Pali: truth. In this poem, truth is one, and there is no second.

carryVoice: Keep this one: each calls it true, me included. Twelve poems of the eights, read.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 4.12 (Culaviyuha Sutta, the Smaller Array)
